newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Amid violence, shaken Nicaraguans call for peace.
newsitem.headline: Amid violence, shaken Nicaraguans call for peace.

text.p: Nicaraguans took to the streets on Wednesday to protest rising political violence that has raised fears the country could slide back into chaos.
Hundreds of Nicaraguans, waving white handkerchiefs for peace, gathered on a central street where hundreds of students have recently waged pitched battles with police.
"We're tired of violence. We must stand up against it," Claudia Paniagua, a civil rights worker, told the crowd.

Some 150 people have been injured in fighting between police and protesters in the last three weeks, and the violence has rattled Nicaraguans -- whose country was torn by civil war for much of its modern history.

Late on Tuesday, masked students seized the ground floor of Managua's international airport, until they were dislodged by police firing rubber bullets. Flights were not disrupted but many travelers were shocked to see protesters wielding home-made weapons in the airport lounge.

Fears that the country -- still polarised between the left-wing Sandinista Front and right-wing rulers -- could slide back into the open conflict that plagued the country from 1979-1990 have set citizens' nerves on edge.
"Is this the country that we want to pass on to our children?" said Gerardo Salinas, head of the country's main private-sector lobbying group Cosep.
Using the slogan, "I want peace," Cosep launched a campaign on Wednesday to halt the conflicts, and called on citizens to carry white ribbons and flags.

The fear of trouble was widely associated with the approaching anniversary of the 1979 Sandinista Revolution on July 19, amid signs the Sandinistas have grown increasingly hostile to the government of rightist President Arnoldo Aleman.
Aleman has called on leaders from all Nicaragua's political, labour and professional groups to take part in a "national dialogue" next week to ease tensions.
But the Sandinistas, led by veteran former revolutionary leader Daniel Ortega who lost to Aleman in elections last November, have said they will not participate.

Instead, Ortega has spoken of a "second phase" of protests, and there were widespread fears his party was planning disruptions in the northern city of Esteli -- an area of much fighting during the Sandinista's civil war against U.S.-backed Contra rebels in the 1980s.
Army troops and police have moved extra units into Esteli, some 60 miles (100 km) north of Managua, in an apparent attempt to forestall trouble.

Army Gen. Joaquin Cuadra said the deployment was due to increased bank robberies and crime. But other military sources, speaking on condition of anonomity, said it followed fears that Sandinista ex-army officers may be planning violence in Esteli.
